title: Mapping of Atypical Cortical Areal Topologies in the Human Brain
title_html: Mapping of Atypical Cortical Areal Topologies in the Human Brain
abstract: Previous studies using the Human Connectome Project Multimodal Parcellation version 1.0 identified atypical topologies of area 55b using MSMAll areal-feature-based registration and a multi-layer perceptron areal classifier. Area 55b was sometimes bisected by neighboring areas FEF or PEF or swapped positions with FEF. These patterns were supported across multiple underlying modalities, including myelin maps, functional connectivity, and task activation, arguing that this variability was genuine. However, the prevalence, reproducibility, and feature determinants of atypical cortical topologies across the full cortex remain largely unexplored. Here, we used an improved deep learning-based surface registration together with a refined multimodal areal classifier that maximizes reproducible individual variability to investigate atypical cortical area topologies in HCP Young Adult (HCP-YA, N=1,071, 22-35 years of age) participants. To assess reproducibility, we additionally analyzed 45 HCP test-retest individuals.Cortical areas were examined for fragmentation and alternative neighbor arrangements. For each cortical area and subject, a fragmentation index [0-1] based on mesh connectivity was computed to quantify split of an area. Zero indicated spatially contiguous areas, whereas higher values reflected multiple fragments. Areas with fragmentation indices within a predefined range [0.1-0.5] were classified as split topologies, while excluding small, isolated vertex clusters which can arise from classifier uncertainty. To evaluate whether observed splits reflect biologically meaningful topologies, the top-ranked multimodal features based on classifier feature importance and their surface gradients were analyzed. Split boundaries were aligned with strong transitions in the underlying multimodal feature maps. Preliminary results indicate robust split topology of area 55b in ~8% of participants, occurring in 41 individuals in the left hemisphere, 45 in the right hemisphere, and 4 bilaterally. Neighbor analyses showed atypical configurations also in adjacent areas such as FEF and PEF, such as 55b splitting area FEF or area PEF. Simultaneous split topologies were also observed, including cases in which both 55b and PEF or both 55b and FEF were split within the same hemisphere. Functional connectivity patterns and their gradients support these atypical configurations, indicating that these findings represent genuine biological variability. Together, these findings characterize atypical cortical area topologies in the human brain and establish a framework for studying individual differences in cortical organization.

title: Probabilistic Functional Modes outperforms Temporal Independent Components Analysis for an fMRI atlas of weighted spatially overlapping functional networks
title_html: Probabilistic Functional Modes outperforms Temporal Independent Components Analysis for an fMRI atlas of weighted spatially overlapping functional networks
abstract: Functional networks (sets of brain regions with synchronized activity fluctuations) are often mapped with fMRI using "winner-take-all" hard parcellations that assign each brain location to a single dominant network and thereby oversimplify the brain's functional organization. Weighted, spatially overlapping decompositions capture this organization more faithfully, but the most widely used approach, spatial independent component analysis (sICA) constrains components to be spatially uncorrelated, which is neurobiologically implausible. Temporal ICA (tICA) and probabilistic functional modes (PFM, or PROFUMO) both relax this constraint (though tICA enforces temporal orthogonality), yet it remains unclear which better supports a reproducible and neurobiologically interpretable atlas. Using high-quality fMRI from the Human Connectome Project Young Adult dataset (3 Tesla, n=1071; 7 Tesla, n=175) across resting, traditional repetitive tasks, movie, and retinotopy states, we compared tICA and PFM to determine which yields a more suitable atlas. We evaluated three dimensions: (1) reproducibility across two independent groups (n=475 each), within test-retest individuals (n=45), and across imaging states, using hierarchical clustering to group corresponding components into cross-state "families"; (2) neurobiological interpretability, by spatially correlating component maps to group-level task general linear model (GLM) activations; and (3) individualization, by the same GLM comparison at the single-subject level. At the group and individual levels, tICA and PFM showed comparable reproducibility, interpretability, and individualization, with tICA holding a slight advantage in some task comparisons. However, tICA tended to split single networks into multiple subcomponents to enforce temporal independence, producing more fragmented correlation structure, whereas PFM yielded cleaner, more coherent component correspondence. PFM also showed stronger cross-state reproducibility, identifying more multi-state component families, and a more stable network structure. Although both methods perform similarly overall, PFM's greater cross-state consistency and more coherent structure make it more suitable for constructing a reproducible and neurobiologically interpretable atlas of weighted, spatially overlapping functional networks

title: A causal and lateralized role of the human amygdala in evidence accumulation under emotional ambiguity
title_html: A causal and lateralized role of the human amygdala in evidence accumulation under emotional ambiguity
abstract: Background: Accumulation-to-bound theories propose that decisions emerge through the gradual integration of noisy evidence toward a decision threshold. Although corticostriatal circuits have been widely implicated in evidence accumulation (EA), the role of the amygdala remains poorly understood. Single-unit recordings suggest that amygdala neurons encode EA signals, whereas neuroimaging studies indicate hemispheric specialization in processing emotional valence and decision ambiguity. However, the causal contribution of the amygdala to EA and its potential lateralization remain unclear. Methods: We combined intracranial electrophysiological recordings (n=15), direct electrical stimulation of the amygdala (n=14 sessions), and focal radiofrequency ablation (RFA; n=7) in neurosurgical patients. Participants completed an emotion interpretation task involving graded perceptual ambiguity. EA was quantified using drift diffusion modeling of choice and reaction time data. Amygdala event-related potentials (ERPs) were analyzed to characterize emotional representations and their relationships with latent EA parameters. Stimulation and RFA were used to test the causal role of amygdala hemispheres and subregions. Results: Computational-neural mapping analyses revealed that amygdala ERP activity occurring 300-500 ms after face onset tracked trial-by-trial drift-rate estimates, identifying a neural signature of EA within the human amygdala. This effect exhibited nuclei- and hemisphere-specific organization: the left amygdala, particularly the lateral and basal nuclei, encoded both emotional valence and ambiguity and showed robust drift-rate representations, whereas the right amygdala primarily encoded ambiguity and exhibited weaker drift-rate modulation, especially in the lateral nucleus. Consistent with these findings, left amygdala stimulation increased drift rate, whereas right amygdala ablation reduced drift rate, providing causal evidence that the amygdala contributes to EA during social-emotional decision-making. Conclusions: These findings provide convergent electrophysiological and causal evidence that the human amygdala contributes directly to evidence accumulation during social-emotional decisions. Our findings extend computational models of decision-making beyond corticostriatal circuits and identify amygdala subnuclei as potential neuromodulation targets for emotional and decision-making dysfunction in psychiatric disorders.

title: A Deep Learning Framework Enables Transcriptomic Characterization from Neuronal Spike Waveform
title_html: A Deep Learning Framework Enables Transcriptomic Characterization from Neuronal Spike Waveform
abstract: Recent advances in single-cell multimodal technologies have presented unique opportunities for measuring multiple characteristics of individual cells including transcriptomics, electrophysiology and morphology. Although many machine learning strategies have been developed that can be employed to integrate and analyze these multimodal datasets for deciphering correlations between transcriptomic characteristics with the electrophysiological features. However, these strategies rely on manually defined feature extraction from various data modalities or dimensionality reduction strategies which are susceptible to instability and poor generalization, especially with the electrophysiological datasets. Here, we demonstrate a deep learning framework that enables transcriptomic cell-type identification from electrophysiological recordings. We found that neuronal spike waveform is sufficient to enable cell-type identification with high accuracy (~95%), thereby alleviating the instability and poor generalization issues associated with previously developed machine learning strategies. The ensemble neural waveform trajectory analysis illustrated the unique upstroke and downstroke trajectory for distinct cell-types demonstrating the richness of information in the spike waveform which is not well realized by manually defined electrophysiological features. We have applied and benchmarked this proposed deep learning framework with two independent datasets collected utilizing different techniques: (1) patch-seq technique and, (2) intracellular electrophysiology form genetically labelled neurons, further demonstrating the ubiquitous applicability of the proposed framework. We envision that such a strategy could be employed to develop a unified framework which can identify the cell-type from the intracellular recordings obtained from unlabeled cells which remain elusive.

title: ABRACADABRA: An automated electrophysiology feature extractor for neuron classification
title_html: ABRACADABRA: An automated electrophysiology feature extractor for neuron classification
abstract:
As we seek to learn more about the complex processes of the nervous system, it will be essential to integrate information about the anatomy, connectivity, gene expression patterns, and function of individual neuronal types. In recent years, technological advancements in single-cell RNA sequencing have enabled tremendous insights into gene expression patterns and distinct cell types throughout the nervous system. While powerful, these large-scale omics datasets often lack information on neuronal function and connectivity. Patch-seq approaches, which combine patch-clamp electrophysiology with single-cell RNA sequencing and morphological reconstructions, help bridge these gaps. However, the analysis of electrophysiological recordings is time consuming and manual analysis can be subjective, making it challenging to standardize large-scale data sets. Efforts to automate feature extraction include open-source packages such as IPFX and pyABF, but they require users to have prior programming expertise.
Here we developed ABRACADABRA, an analysis application with a customizable GUI to efficiently visualize and extract electrophysiological features from current-clamp recordings. ABRACADABRA is designed to use protocol-specific analysis algorithms to standardize extraction of 81 different features from standard step and ramp current injection protocols, all exported in annotated CSV files. We verified the accuracy of ABRACADABRA feature extraction against previously published studies on excitability of human dorsal root ganglion neurons (DRG). Using ABRACADABRA, we systematically analyzed 142 recordings from genetically defined mouse DRG neurons and trained a classification model to predict transcriptomic cell identity from electrophysiological properties. We also show that this analysis pipeline can be used to identify specific classes of human somatosensory neurons based on their electrical properties and understand how these are linked to their transcriptomic identity using Patch-seq recordings. We anticipate that this user-friendly open-source software will enable more rapid and reliable analysis of patch-clamp recording data.

title: Silencing REST by microRNA-153 Reduces Nestin and Increases Doublecortin Expression in Neural Stem Cells: Implications for Alzheimer's Disease and Autism
title_html: Silencing REST by microRNA-153 Reduces Nestin and Increases Doublecortin Expression in Neural Stem Cells: Implications for Alzheimer's Disease and Autism
abstract: Neural stem cell (NSC) differentiation into neural progenitor cells and mature neurons is essential for normal brain development and maintenance. Its dysregulation contributes to neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, molecular regulation of this process remains unclear. Circular RNAs and microRNAs (miRNAs or miR) may play critical roles therein. Among these, miR-153, miR-339, miR-346, and miR-298 have been implicated in regulating several proteins associated with AD pathology. Identifying factors that drive AD pathology and understanding how they regulate the formation of extracellular amyloid plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles are critical for developing novel therapeutic targets. Our research focuses on the regulation of amyloid-β precursor protein (APP), microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT), α-synuclein (SNCA), and repressor element-1 silencing transcription factor (REST), a transcriptional repressor of neuronal genes that is dysregulated during AD. Although REST dysfunction has been linked to neurodegeneration, the mechanisms underlying its post-transcriptional regulation remain poorly understood. REST has also been implicated in ASD through regulating genes involved in neuronal development, synapse formation, and neural circuit function. We demonstrate that miR-153 directly targets the REST 3′-untranslated region (UTR), thereby reducing REST mRNA and protein levels in human cell lines. In addition, miR-153 suppressed APP and SNCA levels, suggesting coordinated regulation of multiple pathways of neurodegenerative diseases. Elevated miR-153 expression was associated with reduced AD risk, whereas increased REST expression correlated with a greater likelihood of disease. During neural differentiation, we observed that the effects of miR-153 were stage-dependent. In NSCs, miR-153 decreased REST and nestin-1 expression while increasing neuronal markers NSE and doublecortin, indicating promotion of neuronal differentiation and neurogenesis. Collectively, we identify miR-153 as a key regulator of REST and other neurodegeneration-associated genes. By coordinating suppression of APP, SNCA, and REST, miR-153 may reduce accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and promote neuronal differentiation. These results highlight the potential of miR-153 as both a biomarker and a therapeutic target for AD and ASD.

title: Pathogenic tau inhibits synaptic plasticity by blocking eIF4B-mediated local protein synthesis
title_html: Pathogenic tau inhibits synaptic plasticity by blocking eIF4B-mediated local protein synthesis
abstract: Activity-dependent modulation of synaptic strength is critical for encoding memories and it is inhibited in tauopathies including Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Frontotemporal lobar degeneration with tau inclusions (FTLD-tau). Pathogenic tau accumulates in neurons where it obstructs synaptic plasticity. How tau blocks synaptic plasticity leading to memory loss is unclear. Here, we used human iPSC-derived neurons to show that FTLD-tau inhibits plasticity by blocking activity-dependent protein synthesis in dendrites. In the plasticity-associated translatome, we identified a subset of downregulated translated mRNAs in FTLD-tau neurons that encode postsynaptic plasticity regulators. Activity-induced protein synthesis in FTLD-tau neurons was blocked by tau binding to eIF4B which caused eIF4B dissociation from the translation initiation complex and reduced dendritic eIF4B levels. We show in the PS19 tauopathy mouse model that eIF4B protein levels are reduced in the molecular layer of the dentate gyrus. Expression of eIF4B in the hippocampus restores synaptic plasticity and memory performance in PS19 mice. Inhibiting the tau-eIF4B interaction or enhancing eIF4B levels in human FTLD-tau neurons restored local protein synthesis and synaptic plasticity. Together, this suggests that pathogenic tau binding to eIF4B disables the local synthesis of plasticity-related proteins that drive synapse strengthening and memory formation.

title: Investigating the role of tau pre-formed fibrils in exacerbating alpha synuclein-induced neurotoxicity
title_html: Investigating the role of tau pre-formed fibrils in exacerbating alpha synuclein-induced neurotoxicity
abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder affecting over 10 million people worldwide and represents a major public health burden due to its increasing prevalence and lack of disease-modifying therapies available. Although aggregation of α-synuclein into Lewy bodies is a defining feature of PD, growing evidence indicates that mixed proteinopathies are common, with hyperphosphorylated tau frequently co-localizing with α-synuclein aggregates. These overlapping protein accumulations are associated with accelerated cognitive decline and worse clinical outcomes, yet the mechanistic role of tau in α-syn-mediated toxicity remains poorly understood. Elucidating this interaction is therefore critical for improving our understanding of disease progression and identifying new therapeutic targets. Here, we propose that tau pre-formed fibrils (PFFs) potentiate α-syn PFF-induced glutamatergic dysregulation and excitotoxic signaling, resulting in enhanced neurotoxicity compared to either protein alone. Specifically, we will test whether combined α-syn and tau pathology leads to greater excitotoxic signaling, as reflected by increased calcium influx and elevated glutamate levels, relative to single-protein conditions. We hypothesize that tau PFFs act synergistically with α-syn PFFs to exacerbate neuronal dysfunction through dysregulation of glutamatergic signaling pathways. Overall, these findings will provide mechanistic insight into neurodegeneration in mixed proteinopathies and to identify pathways that may be targeted for therapeutic intervention in PD and related neurodegenerative disorders.

Here, we propose that tau pre-formed fibrils (PFFs) potentiate α-syn PFF-induced glutamatergic dysregulation and excitotoxic signaling, resulting in enhanced neurotoxicity compared to either protein alone. Specifically, we will test whether combined α-syn and tau pathology leads to greater excitotoxic signaling, as reflected by increased calcium influx and elevated glutamate levels, relative to single-protein conditions. We hypothesize that tau PFFs act synergistically with α-syn PFFs to exacerbate neuronal dysfunction through dysregulation of glutamatergic signaling pathways. Overall, these findings will provide mechanistic insight into neurodegeneration in mixed proteinopathies and to identify pathways that may be targeted for therapeutic intervention in PD and related neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Shining a new light into recovery of brain functioning following a mild Traumatic Brain Injury: Using Photobiomodulation therapy to examine cortical functioning differences during n-back task performance
title_html: Shining a new light into recovery of brain functioning following a mild Traumatic Brain Injury: Using Photobiomodulation therapy to examine cortical functioning differences during n-back task performance
abstract: Mild Traumatic Brain Injuries (mTBIs) involve impact to the head that is commonly caused by motor vehicle accidents, sports or recreational activities, work-related injuries, or falling. At injury occurrence, the impact to the head can often result in somatic, cognitive, sensory, and psychological issues. A mTBI can result in disruption of brain functioning and cognitive disturbances. While many patients can often experience a full recovery following a mTBI, other people may experience a longer recovery time, and lingering effects can persist still in many individuals. Effective recovery of brain functioning following mTBI can help individuals return to normal activities, but treatment options remain limited in this population. Photobiomodulation (PBM) is a low-level laser therapy that can be applied directly onto the head and is hypothesized to improve neural functioning and cognitive performance. In a randomized double-blinded feasibility study, we investigated if PBM treatment promotes recovery of brain functioning during cognitive performance following mTBI. Fifteen individuals with a recent mTBI (<3 months) were randomly assigned to either a PBM treatment at 810 nm (n = 8) or sham/control group (n = 7) for six sessions over two weeks. Before and after the intervention, participants completed a computerized N-Back task (testing working memory) while dense electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings were obtained. Event-Related Potentials (ERPs) were derived from the EEG, and the Low-Resolution Electromagnetic Tomography (LORETA) method was applied to estimate cortical activity during task performance. Analyses of variance revealed a significant time (pre, post) X group (PBM, placebo) interaction for the right temporal and right limbic cortex activity during the N1 and P3 ERP component time windows respectively for the 1 back match trials (right temporal at N1: p = 0.017, ƞp2= 0.365; right limbic at P3: p = 0.002, ƞp2= 0.585). This interaction was explained by a reduction in cortical activity in the PBM group, in contrast to an increase in cortical activity in the placebo group from pre- to post-treatment. The findings provide preliminary evidence that PBM therapy promoted more efficient cortical activity during working memory processes compared to placebo, potentially reflecting a PBM-induced return to pre-injury functioning.

title: Brain-wide circuits for competing prey processing in larval zebrafish
title_html: Brain-wide circuits for competing prey processing in larval zebrafish
abstract: Animals often must choose one object for action while ignoring other simultaneously available stimuli. Prey hunting provides a natural setting for studying this problem. Larval zebrafish frequently encounter multiple prey and must orient toward and capture one selected prey item, the target, even when other prey are present. Using this model system, we asked how the brain represents this competition context, defined here as whether hunting occurs with a single prey item or with multiple competing prey. Behaviorally, competing prey reduced capture success and biased the fish’s initial orienting turn, indicating disrupted target selection. Brain-wide calcium imaging revealed widespread suppression of neuronal activity evoked by the selected prey, with the strongest effects in the habenula and nucleus isthmi. Population analyses showed regional specialization: the optic tectum primarily encoded target location, whereas the nucleus isthmi and habenula encoded competition context, and habenula was the earliest predictor of behavioral outcome. Competition and outcome also reshaped inter-areal communication. Habenula ablation impaired hunting, weakened inter-areal communication, and disrupted competition-related representations, particularly in the nucleus isthmi. These results reveal a brain-wide circuit mechanism for selecting among competing stimuli and identify the habenula as a key node linking sensory competition to behavioral engagement.

title: Childhood Emotional Maltreatment Predicts Nicotine Dependence and Resting-State Self-Control Connectivity in Adults who Smoke Daily
title_html: Childhood Emotional Maltreatment Predicts Nicotine Dependence and Resting-State Self-Control Connectivity in Adults who Smoke Daily
abstract: Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) have emerged as important risk factors for substance use and nicotine dependence, yet neurobiological mechanisms linking early emotional maltreatment to nicotine dependence remain unclear. Emerging evidence further suggests that ACEs are associated with alterations in wide-scale differences in brain connectivity in cortical networks implicated in cognitive and emotional regulation. We examined whether a factor indexing childhood emotional maltreatment predicted nicotine dependence severity and brain connectivity measures in adult daily smokers.Adults who smoked daily (N=46) completed two counterbalanced fMRI sessions — one following 24-hour abstinence, one following ad lib smoking — plus baseline assessments including the Maltreatment and Abuse Chronology of Exposure (MACE) and Fagerström Test for Nicotine Dependence (FTND). A four-subscale emotional maltreatment (EM) factor (emotional neglect, non-verbal emotional abuse, parental verbal abuse, peer emotional abuse) was derived from the MACE via factor analysis in an independent community sample (n=261; 61% variance explained) and projected onto study participants. rIFG-preSMA connectivity, a circuit involved in response inhibition (Schaum et al., 2021) and the Resource Allocation Index (RAI), an index of large-scale network coupling (Lerman et al., 2014), were examined using linear mixed-effects models covarying session and head motion. The EM factor predicted nicotine dependence severity (r=+.43, p=.006). Higher EM was associated with weaker rIFG-preSMA connectivity in the sated state (r=−.42, p=.014), but there was no effect of session on rIFG-preSMA connectivity (p=0.17). RAI was significantly different between nicotine abstinent and sated sessions (β=−0.23, p=.002), replicating previous results, but this difference was not related to EM (β=+0.02, p=.68). Childhood EM predicts nicotine dependence and reduced connectivity in a self-control circuit under sated conditions. Its dissociation from RAI, a state-sensitive index of large-scale network allocation, suggests a stable trait marker of self-regulatory circuitry rather than a withdrawal-related state effect, implicating disrupted inhibitory control circuitry as a neurobiological pathway linking early adversity to enduring nicotine dependence.

title: Motion-Energy Modeling Predicts and Decodes Naturalistic Visual Representations in Mouse Cortex
title_html: Motion-Energy Modeling Predicts and Decodes Naturalistic Visual Representations in Mouse Cortex
abstract: Introduction: Natural vision requires animals to extract behaviorally relevant information from dynamic scenes, yet mouse visual cortex is often studied with simplified stimuli that isolate receptive-field properties but omit natural spatiotemporal structure. We asked whether a motion-energy encoding framework can preserve the complexity of natural movies while retaining interpretable links to classical visual features. Methods: Awake head-fixed GCaMP4.3 mice (n=5) underwent one-photon wide-field calcium imaging during natural-movie viewing. Each mouse viewed 90 min of unique training movies and 10 repeats of a held-out 9-min test movie. title: Scale Invariance in Economic Choices: Behavioral Evidence, Neuronal Origins, and Decision Models
title_html: Scale Invariance in Economic Choices: Behavioral Evidence, Neuronal Origins, and Decision Models
abstract:
It is often assumed that economic choices are driven by the value difference. Here we examined 16 data sets from 9 rhesus monkeys performing 7 different tasks. Consistently, choices were better explained as driven by the log value ratio - a trait termed scale invariance. In principle, scale invariance might be imposed by sublinear value functions (Weber-Fechner law). However, value-encoding neurons in orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), whose activity is causal to choices, represent values linearly (Rustichini et al., 2017). Hence, we propose that scale invariance emerges during value comparison. We then examined three leading models describing this process - a biophysically realistic model of spiking cells (Wang, 2002), the mutual inhibition model (Wong and Wang, 2006; Hunt et al., 2012), and the drift-diffusion model (Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008; Krajbich et al., 2010). In their standard version, which assumes that input noise is independent of input strength, all three models fail to account for scale invariance. However, if input noise is assumed proportional to the input strength (Poisson variability), as observed in OFC neurons encoding the offer values (Tolhurst et al., 1983; Conen and Padoa-Schioppa, 2015), all three models closely reproduce scale invariance. The theory presented here provides a new interpretation for the Weber-Fechner phenomenon in the context of economic decisions.
References:

title: Modeling and analyzing the role of oscillations in encoding sequential memories
title_html: Modeling and analyzing the role of oscillations in encoding sequential memories
abstract: Oscillations are a ubiquitous feature of neural activity, present at rest and during cognitive tasks, even those devoid of overt periodic structure. Yet, the functional meaning of these oscillations remains unclear. While substantial insight has been gleaned as to the biophysical mechanisms by which neural oscillations are generated, less is known about why such oscillations manifest and the extent to which they are causally related to neural computation. From a theoretical perspective, it is known that models with oscillatory priors can be optimized or trained to perform complex tasks, establishing a level of sufficiency for oscillation-based computation. But, are such dynamics also necessary? Here, we interrogate this question through mathematical reasoning and top-down studies of neural network models. Our specific formulation is in the domain of working memory, as a surrogate for core cognitive function. We argue that in this domain, oscillatory dynamics are a natural solution for generalizable and scalable maintenance of memoranda. We then show that networks trained on a complex, combinatorial working memory pattern completion task overwhelmingly find such dynamics as a preferred solution. Interestingly, such networks are significantly aided by the presence of transmission delays, such as those found in biological circuits. This indicates that these latencies may act as an important structural regularizer that steers the network toward these functionally favorable dynamics.

title: A Trio of Brain Networks Orchestrates Music Recognition
title_html: A Trio of Brain Networks Orchestrates Music Recognition
abstract: Recognition memory continuously integrates internal representations with sensory information to guide adaptive behavior. Yet most theoretical models conceptualize recognition as a discrete sequence of steps, involving sensory processing, hippocampal retrieval, and cortical reinstatement. However, in natural settings, perception, memory, and predictions interact continuously within an evolving context to guide adaptive responses. Consequently, it remains unclear how distributed brain networks coordinate the integration of internal and external information during dynamic recognition. Here, we combined intracranial recordings (N = 30) of high-frequency activity (70-160 Hz) and dimensionality reduction to characterize whole-brain network dynamics during music recognition. We identified three interacting functional networks supporting sensory processing, sensory-memory integration, and decision formation, whose temporal dynamics predicted the timing of behavior. During recognition of learned sequences, sensory activity progressively attenuated, the integrative network combined sensory inputs with mnemonic and contextual information, and decision related activity-gradually evolved toward behavioral engagement. Novel sequences disrupted this organization by sustaining sensory responses and accelerating decision-related activity. Information exchange was structured rather than uniform: sensory and integrative networks communicated bidirectionally, whereas decision-related activity exerted selective top-down influences on sensory processing. Our findings reveal recognition as a distributed, context-dependent, and goal-directed process emerging from the continuous coordination of large-scale brain networks.

title: Hippocampal substantia nigra dopamine reinforces reward-related long-term memories
title_html: Hippocampal substantia nigra dopamine reinforces reward-related long-term memories
abstract: Dopamine signaling has been primarily studied in the striatum, leaving its functions in other brain regions poorly understood despite widespread dopaminergic innervation. Although dopamine is required for long-term memory in the hippocampus, technical challenges in directly measuring dopamine release during behavior have left the source and role of hippocampal dopamine signals unresolved. Using simultaneous optical dopamine measurement and temporally precise, physiologically titrated optogenetic manipulation during behavior, we identify substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) as a major source of reward-associated dopamine transients in dorsal CA1. In a hidden reward zone task, these transients were tightly coupled to rewarded licking bouts, consistent with an action-related signal at reward collection. We hypothesized that this signal reinforces reward-related information during learning. Brief suppression of SNc dopaminergic inputs during the post-reward period reduced the dopamine transient and impaired memory for goal location tested 24 hr later, demonstrating the necessity of this signal. Control manipulations delivered earlier on the track or during dark time had no effect. Conversely, boosting SNc dopamine release at rewards augmented reward transients and enhanced next day memory. Together, these findings identify a surprising role for SNc dopaminergic action signals in reinforcing hippocampal reward-related information during the formation of long-term memories. Furthermore, these discoveries suggest a potential circuit link between the loss of hippocampal SNc dopaminergic inputs and the cognitive impairment often seen in Parkinson's disease.

title: A single dynamical property can account for the capacity to learn, from artificial networks to the mammalian brain
title_html: A single dynamical property can account for the capacity to learn, from artificial networks to the mammalian brain
abstract:
Every brain must adapt to an unpredictable world, yet individuals differ in how readily they learn. Theoretical work in neuroscience and machine learning suggests that learning is fastest when a system is initialized close to instability — i.e., near criticality — because such systems support a diverse repertoire of patterns and multi-scale correlations that promote information propagation.
Here, we empirically estimate an individual's distance to criticality and ask whether it predicts subsequent motor learning. In adult WT mice (N=18), we recorded single-unit activity in primary motor cortex for 24-48 hours in the baseline period. Then, we exposed mice to two six-day motor tasks: prey capture and ladder crossing. Using a renormalization-group-based measure of proximity to criticality (d2), we found that mice closer to criticality learned both tasks faster (prey capture: r²=0.74; ladder gait acquisition: r²=0.61), even though d2 predicted neither naive performance nor asymptotic skill. Thus, d2 a specific predictive power on learning rate. Mice closer to criticality also paired a broader repertoire of ladder-crossing exploration with a more tightly consolidated successful gait, linking criticality to the explore-exploit tradeoff during skill acquisition. In the visual cortex of anesthetized ferret kits (N=14), baseline d2 also predicted the magnitude of experience-dependent shifts in direction selectivity following patterned visual stimulation (r²=0.54), exceeding all comparator features. A minimal recurrent network model reproduces these effects: proximity to criticality sets the timescale over which a system can assign credit to past experience, directly setting the rate of learning. Together, these results show that proximity to criticality can account for the capacity to learn, from artificial networks to the mammalian brain.

title: Identification of an evolutionarily conserved intronic enhancer regulating expression of the norepinephrine synthesis enzyme dopamine β-hydroxylase
title_html: Identification of an evolutionarily conserved intronic enhancer regulating expression of the norepinephrine synthesis enzyme dopamine β-hydroxylase
abstract: The critical catecholamine norepinephrine (NE) is produced by small populations of noradrenergic cells located in the brainstem, sympathetic chain, and adrenal medulla. Despite their limited numbers, these cells have an outsized impact on diverse behaviors and physiological drives, including arousal, stress responses, and autonomic function. Dysregulation of NE synthesis in the locus coeruleus, the largest population of noradrenergic neurons in the brain, has been implicated in numerous psychiatric, neurodevelopmental, and neurodegenerative disorders, highlighting the importance of understanding the regulation of NE synthesis. Identifying factors that contribute to variations in NE levels are crucial for identifying vulnerabilities to neurological disorders and may reveal novel therapeutic targets. The enzyme responsible for the final step in NE synthesis is dopamine β-hydroxylase, encoded by the DBH gene, which catalyzes the conversion of dopamine to NE. Our lab generated a floxed allele of mouse Dbh which unexpectedly exhibited reduced Dbh mRNA levels in both central and peripheral noradrenergic cells in the absence of Cre recombination. NE was also reduced in the brain, but not in the adrenal medulla or plasma. Sequence analysis indicates that the insertion of a loxP site in intron 1 of Dbh interrupted an evolutionarily conserved sequence element located within a larger putative enhancer that is present in both mouse and human DBH genes. We employed CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) and ATAC-seq in Dbh-expressing mouse neuroblastoma cells to assess the activity of this putative enhancer region and further characterize its capacity to regulate Dbh transcription. We found that CRISPRi of sequences within the conserved region significantly decreased Dbh and induced a closed chromatin conformation at the target site. Similar targeting of the orthologous region in human neuroblastoma cells significantly reduced DBH mRNA and protein expression, demonstrating an evolutionarily conserved role for this enhancer in regulating DBH expression. Together, these findings identify a conserved genetic regulatory element that influences DBH expression and may contribute to individual variation in NE synthesis. Ongoing studies are investigating the functional consequences of enhancer perturbation on NE production, the broader chromatin landscape and transcriptional networks influenced by this regulatory element, and the capacity of enhancer activation to increase DBH expression. Future work will also examine whether known genetic variants within this conserved region alter DBH expression and contribute to altered NE synthesis.

title: Characterizing the Metabolic Effects of Dietary Fiber Types and ApoE Isoforms in Mice
title_html: Characterizing the Metabolic Effects of Dietary Fiber Types and ApoE Isoforms in Mice
abstract: The gut microbiome plays an important role in human metabolism, nutrition, physiology, and immune function. Accumulating evidence suggests that imbalances in the normal gut microbiome are linked to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) through the regulation of microbiome-associated metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). These findings suggest that reconditioning the gut microbiome may represent a novel strategy for treating the disease.Soluble dietary fiber (SDF) is a fermentable carbohydrate found in plant-based foods that cannot be digested by human enzymes in the small intestine. However, once SDF reaches the large intestine, it can be selectively metabolized by the gut microbiota. Additionally, recent studies have indicated that Apolipoprotein E genotype (APOE) genotype, the strongest common genetic risk factor for AD, influences the structure of the gut microbiome. This raises the question of whether APOE isoforms differentially influence the impact of SDF intake on metabolism, immunity, and brain function synergistically with the gut microbiota.Here, we tested whether soluble dietary fiber could modulate gut microbiome composition and associated metabolite production in an APOE genotype-dependent manner. Mice expressing human APOE3 or APOE4 were randomly assigned to two dietary groups and fed either custom SDF-free or -rich diets for 1.5 months beginning at 2 months of age. Targeted metabolomic analysis revealed that the main SCFAs—acetate, propionate, and butyrate—were significantly higher in APOE4 mice than in APOE3 mice across diet types. (genotype effect, p < 0.05). Propionate and butyrate levels were also significantly higher in mice fed the SDF-rich diet compared with those fed the SDF-free diet (diet-type effect, p < 0.05). Additionally, 16S rRNA-based microbiome analysis revealed microbial community shifts associated with both diet type and genotype. E.g., Romboutsia ilealis was significantly more abundant in mice fed the SDF-free diet than in those fed the SDF-rich diet, whereas Erysipelotrichaceae Allobaculum was significantly more abundant in mice fed the SDF-rich diet than in those fed the SDF-free diet. Both taxa were more abundant in APOE4 mice than in APOE3 mice.Currently, we are evaluating factors involved in neuroinflammation and other brain functions and attempting to integrate these findings with microbiome and metabolome data to provide a holistic understanding of these complex interactions. Finally, we will discuss the implications of these findings for AD and future directions.

title: Encoding of binocular disparity by narrow-field neurons in the mouse superior colliculus
title_html: Encoding of binocular disparity by narrow-field neurons in the mouse superior colliculus
abstract: To capture prey, animals must localize rapidly moving targets in three dimensions and strikewithin a narrow range of distances. Binocular disparity — the oﬀset between the two eyes'images of an object — is a powerful cue for distance, but where and how the brain extractsdisparity to guide rapid orienBng behavior is incompletely understood. While stereoscopicdepth percepBon is generally aDributed to recurrent corBcal processing, its demands may betoo slow to support ballisBc acBons. The superior colliculus (SC) is a conserved sensorimotorhub required for prey capture in mice, and its narrow-ﬁeld (NF) neurons have been implicated indriving predatory behavior. Whether and how NF neurons compute binocular disparity,however, remains unknown. A neuron tuned to crossed disparity must integrate inputs fromnon-corresponding locaBons in the two eyes, predicBng that its monocular recepBve ﬁelds (RFs)should be spaBally oﬀset. Here, we test this predicBon by recording from NF neurons in the SCof awake mice and mapping their spaBal RFs under interleaved binocular, ipsilateral-only, andcontralateral-only viewing on a hemispherical dome. We ﬁnd that NF neurons exhibitsystemaBcally oﬀset monocular RFs: the contralateral RF anchors the binocular RF posiBon,while the ipsilateral RF is shiRed nasally in azimuth, generaBng tuning for crossed disparity. Eye-tracking and geometric controls conﬁrm that these oﬀsets reﬂect circuit architecture ratherthan eye movements or apparatus misalignment. ConverBng the oﬀsets into preferred objectdistances reveals a populaBon tuned to near space, with a median distance of ~4 cm —matching the stereotyped bite-and-grab strike distance — and a tail extending to ~20 cm acrossthe broader pursuit range. Two independent measurements, comparing contralateral-versus-ipsilateral and binocular-versus-ipsilateral RFs, converge on this tuning. By integraBngmonocular inputs with systemaBc spaBal oﬀsets, SC narrow-ﬁeld neurons compute crossedbinocular disparity to deﬁne the depth dimension of a three-dimensional acBon volume for preycapture.

title: Widespread cortical high-frequency activity during spatial attention is aligned to pulvinar theta phase in human iEEG
title_html: Widespread cortical high-frequency activity during spatial attention is aligned to pulvinar theta phase in human iEEG
abstract:
Modulation of high-frequency activity (HFA) underlies many cognitive processes, in particular selective attention. Attention in general provides salient signals to investigate the larger question of how different cortical and subcortical brain regions interact during cognitive processes. A particular feature of interest is that HFA, even when observed across large cortical regions, tends to be phase-locked to low-frequency rhythms, particularly in the theta (4-8 Hz) range. However, the mechanisms underlying this synchronization of HFA across distributed brain regions remain unclear, especially in the cases of cortical areas that only have weak direct connections. We hypothesize that higher-order thalamic nuclei—especially the pulvinar—play a key role in coordinating this long-range synchronization by entraining outgoing signals to separate cortical regions through theta-band oscillations.
Here, we approach this question in intracranial recordings in humans. We analyzed cortical and thalamic responses from intracranial electrodes implanted in 12 epilepsy patients while they performed a visual spatial attention task (i.e. Egly-Driver task) where visual cues signaled the likely location of upcoming targets. We preprocessed this data using data-driven, clustering-based referencing, which identifies both unique and structurally shared signals in iEEG recordings. We then used a previously described algorithm to identify short-duration, high-amplitude bursts of HFA (which are comparable but use a more general definition than ripples described in the literature).
We observe that both cue and target presentation reliably elicits theta oscillations in the pulvinar and HFA bursts across multiple cortical regions. Furthermore, we find that cortical bursts are significantly phase-locked to the rising phase of pulvinar theta, and that pulvinar theta is stronger when bursts co-occur in multiple regions. We interpret this result as a processing cascade where pulvinar theta is used to synchronize cortical bursts, which in turn reinforce the theta oscillation in thalamus. Additionally, we see that theta phase extracted from different pulvinar subnuclei is locked to bursts in different cortical subnetworks, reflecting underlying thalamocortical connectivity. Finally, we present preliminary results that there is homogeneity among the properties of bursts that may vary depending on the brain region and networks they are a part of. These findings provide novel insight into the role of the thalamus in coordinating cortical activity during attention by leveraging low-frequency oscillations to facilitate inter-areal communication.

title: Dissociation between neural representation of local and global scene segmentation cues
title_html: Dissociation between neural representation of local and global scene segmentation cues
abstract: To make sense of the world around us, the visual system must segment complex visual scenes into an organized representation of distinct object surfaces. Scene segmentation signals are prominent in the primate visual cortex. A substantial proportion of neurons in visual cortical Areas V2 and V4 signal border ownership, i.e. which side of a border is owned by a foreground surface. Psychophysics studies suggest that scene segmentation is informed by cues such as contour junctions. A prominent type of contour junction is the T-junction, which is formed where a border of an occluded surface meets that of an occluding surface. The resulting ‘T’ shape is informative about the depth order of the surfaces: the stem of the T points away from the occluding surface. How the visual system represents T-junctions and how these signals relate to the neural representation of border ownership remains poorly understood. Here we investigate this question by directly comparing the neural representation for border ownership and for T-junction orientation. We recorded spike rates from single and multi-units in visual areas V4 and V2 using Neuropixels probes in a male macaque. After measuring the classical receptive fields (cRFs) of the neurons, we presented three types of scenes during passive fixation. First, classical border ownership scenes, in which the cRFs only contained a luminance border which could be owned by a square surface on one or the other side (Square scenes). Second, scenes in which the cRFs only contained an isolated T-junction (Tj-cropped). Third, stimuli in which identical T-junctions as in Tj-cropped scenes were part of a more elaborate scene (a pair of occluding squares; Tj-squares). Each type of scene was presented at 8-12 orientations, and with different possibilities for the contrast polarity across the borders in the scene. We find that a substantial proportion of units are tuned to the orientation of T-junctions in Tj-cropped scenes. We find that the tuning for T-junction orientation is significantly correlated between Tj-cropped and Tj-squares scenes for V2 units, but not for V4 units. In contrast, in V4, and also in V2, we find a significant correlation between the preferred orientation of border ownership between Square scenes and Tj-squares scenes. In neither area we find a significant correlation between the tuning for T-junction orientation in Tj-cropped scenes and border ownership tuning in Square scenes. Together, our data suggest a dissociation in the representation of local and global scene segmentation cues, with a shift in dominance from a more local to a more global representation between V2 and V4.

title: Early Slow-Wave Sleep Gains as a Marker of Antidepressant Response During Electroconvulsive Therapy
title_html: Early Slow-Wave Sleep Gains as a Marker of Antidepressant Response During Electroconvulsive Therapy
abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is an established and highly effective treatment for patients with severe depression. However, its mechanisms of action remain incompletely understood, and objective early markers of antidepressant response are still needed. Slow-wave sleep (SWS) plays an important role in synaptic plasticity that may be relevant to antidepressant recovery. We examined whether early changes in SWS during ECT were associated with changes in depression severity. Twenty-two participants undergoing an index course of ECT in an ongoing longitudinal study, DNS-ECT, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05905705, completed overnight sleep EEG recordings and Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) assessments over the course of therapy. We examined whether early change in SWS, measured from baseline to two weeks after ECT initiation as a percentage of total sleep time, was associated with change in depression severity from baseline to the end of the ECT course. To account for potential heterogeneity in treatment response, we used a two-component Gaussian mixture model to identify latent response phenotypes based on changes in SWS and MADRS scores. Within each phenotype, we assessed the association between SWS change and MADRS change using Pearson and Spearman correlations. We then used multiple linear regression to test whether the association between SWS change and MADRS change differed by phenotype. MADRS scores decreased substantially by the end of the ECT course, with a mean reduction of 14.1 points from baseline (paired t = 7.30, p < 0.0001). Mean (SD) SWS increased from 60.0 (54.8) to 83.8 (82.6) minutes (Δ = +24.3 minutes, +6.2 %) from baseline to week 2. The mixture model identified two response phenotypes of similar size (n = 12 and n = 10) that did not differ at baseline in age, sex, MADRS, QIDS, or SWS (all p > 0.30). Within both phenotypes, greater SWS gains were strongly associated with greater MADRS reductions. Phenotype 1 showed a slope of −0.92, Pearson r = −0.86, p = 0.0004; phenotype 2 showed a slope of −0.44, Pearson r = −0.85, p = 0.002. The combined model explained 79% of the variance in MADRS change (overall p < 0.0001). Phenotypes differed in coupling magnitude but not direction (interaction p = 0.024; likelihood-ratio p = 0.012). Early gains in SWS during the first two weeks of ECT were closely coupled to subsequent reductions in depression severity assessed at the end of the ECT course across two latent response phenotypes, supporting a consistent relationship between SWS enhancement and antidepressant response. Larger studies are needed to replicate these findings and identify prospective markers of phenotype membership.

title: Why do we seek information about the future? On the origins of subjective value without instrumental value
title_html: Why do we seek information about the future? On the origins of subjective value without instrumental value
abstract: Why do we want to know the future? Humans and many animals pay for information to predict uncertain rewards, even when they cannot control them. The reason for this conserved yet seemingly paradoxical preference - “subjective value without instrumental value” - remains unknown. Here we develop a normative framework to explain the origin of such preferences, their persistence across species, and their contributions to survival. We formalize and evaluate theories that explain information’s subjective value as originating as an adaptive estimate of its advantage for solving core computational problems posed by natural environments. One theory, which we call Time Allocation (TA) theory, proposes that information helps organisms in nature improve their time allocation during foraging (Vasconcelos et al., 2015). A second theory, Credit Assignment (CA) theory, proposes that information helps organisms solve the temporal credit assignment problem during reinforcement learning (Bromberg-Martin and Hikosaka, 2009). We embody each theory with a computational model of an optimal Bayesian agent maximizing reward in a naturalistic environment. We then compute the instrumental value of information in each model, and test whether it predicts the true subjective value of information measured experimentally in humans and monkeys (Bromberg-Martin and Feng et al, 2024). We show that these theories operate through distinct mechanisms, yet remarkably, both make a series of common, correct, detailed predictions about human and animal subjective values. This suggests that organisms may place subjective value on information in order to help them to solve both the TA and CA problems simultaneously in nature. We further leverage our framework to derive novel types of information making it possible to dissociate these theories and test if organisms use a mixture of both to compute their subjective values. Indeed, we show that mixed value computations combining both theories achieve the highest performance across diverse naturalistic environments. Finally, we provide evidence that the theorized benefits of information can also apply to artificial neural network (ANN) agents for reinforcement learning, substantially improving both training speed and performance. Thus, our work provides new evidence that organisms compute the subjective value of information in a manner that is non-instrumental in experimental tasks but is conserved across species and well suited to guide adaptive behavior across a range of natural environments.

title: Burst-driven learning in the human medial temporal lobe
title_html: Burst-driven learning in the human medial temporal lobe
abstract: Neuronal bursts, defined as brief epochs of high-frequency spiking, are known to play a key role in the formation of memory engrams in rodents, where they drive synaptic plasticity more effectively than isolated spikes. However, whether burst-driven learning also occurs in humans, and the time scales at which bursts drive plasticity in humans, is not well understood. A central challenge is that human memory unfolds during active vision, as observers shift their gaze to sample visual information every 200-300 milliseconds, making it difficult to know what information a given burst encodes. To study this question, we collected simultaneous gaze and Medial Temporal Lobe (MTL) single-neuron recordings from epilepsy patients while they performed an old/new recognition task on natural scene images. We parsed burst events from the spike trains and aligned them temporally with the observer’s fixations to obtain precise measurements of what information was being sampled during neuronal bursting and relate burst activity directly to memory outcomes. Our analyses revealed that: (1) bursts occur preferentially when the observer fixates novel visual information, suggesting bursting is gated by the stimulus novelty during natural viewing, (2) during encoding, bursts carve ‘attractor-like’ basins in the neural state space to strengthen subsequent reinstatement of the encoding neural state, (3) burst sharpen the geometry of memory representations at the population level, separating competing memories and enhancing stored pattern retrieval. Further, a burst-gated Modern Hopfield Network reproduces these dynamics, recapitulating recognition behavior and revealing burst-gating as a sufficient computational mechanism for memory storage and retrieval. Taken together, these results suggest that bursts act as a fixation time-scale plasticity mechanism that supports one-shot learning of complex visual content during natural visual exploration and point to burst-gated plasticity as a unifying principle linking rodent and human memory research.

title: NeuroAI-Bench and NeuroAI-Agent: a framework for autonomous neuroscience analysis and exploration
title_html: NeuroAI-Bench and NeuroAI-Agent: a framework for autonomous neuroscience analysis and exploration
abstract:
AI coding agents are entering scientific work yet have mainly been designed and tested for software-engineering tasks. Whether coding agents can reliably analyze and explore complex neuroscience datasets and return trustworthy results is an open question. Rigorous analysis takes more than running code; scientific exploration proceeds through many iterations and field-specific workflows, and interpreting each result properly requires knowledge of the underlying biology, not just skill in data analytics.
To enable autonomous analyses in neuroscience, we first built NeuroAI-Bench, the first benchmark of its kind in the field, which we assembled from published and unpublished datasets and accompanying analyses vetted by human domain experts. It comprises >30 tasks across >15 datasets and >500,000 neurons spanning different species and recording modalities, covering data quality control, inferential analysis, method selection, hypothesis testing, and audit of flawed analyses. Each task specifies a scientific question, the dataset to be used, and the required deliverables, allowing agents to infer suitable methods, controls, and interpretations. Grading of agent performance combines deterministic checks on the outputs with expert rubrics that assess scientific reasoning. In tests of whether off-the-shelf coding tools such as Claude Code and Codex could solve these tasks, we found that they struggled to follow the scientific intent, were harder to steer even with customization efforts, and, when they did produce an answer, left fewer traces of how the results were achieved.
We then built NeuroAI-Agent, an open framework whose execution is restricted to pre-approved analysis tools and workflows that are already accepted in the field. It runs several workflows that are performed by digitized personas from a neuroscience lab. We used different AI agents that respectively play a neuroscientist, a data scientist, a librarian that searches the published literature through vector embeddings, a data engineer that prepares and checks the data, and analysts, statisticians, and reviewers. These personas are stacked to mimic how neuroscientists typically work, down to formulating results and reaching conclusions, and the workflows include predefined cross-specialty iteration loops, such as a neuroscientist agent evaluating a statistician agent's output. Every result carries a full audit trail of how it was produced. On NeuroAI-Bench, this system outperformed off-the-shelf coding tools while adding complete traceability. We intend this work to seed further development toward autonomous, trustworthy, and fully traceable neuroscience analysis at scale.

title: Post Transcriptional regulation in the landscape of aging and nerve injury
title_html: Post Transcriptional regulation in the landscape of aging and nerve injury
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal motor neuron disease (MND) characterized by progressive neurodegeneration and TDP-43 pathology. While transcriptional dysregulation is characteristic of ALS, the post-transcriptional mechanisms that amplify and cause neuronal dysfunction remain poorly understood. We recently studied the role of alternative polyadenylation (APA) as a crucial post-transcriptional mechanism linking TDP-43 dysfunction to MND pathogenesis in neuronal cell models and in ALS postmortem tissue. We found that APA dysregulation drives altered 3′ UTR landscapes and aberrant isoform expression in human neurons. These APA-driven changes impact mRNA stability and subcellular localization of disease-relevant transcripts, underscoring the functional relevance of TDP-43-mediated APA.Building on this work, we are now disentangling post-transcriptional regulation observed in the context of TDP-43 depletion from the changes that are observed in the context of aging and nerve injury. Our preliminary data suggest that APA dysregulation is not only a downstream consequence of TDP-43 pathology, but also a coordinated mechanism by which human neurons respond to injury and normal aging. Using a mouse model of sciatic nerve crush we observed a striking shift towards proximal polyadenylation sites (PASs) (70%) shortly after injury followed by a shift towards distal PASs (77%) during the recovery phase. In a parallel study, we found a global shift towards distal PASs in transdifferentiated (‘aged’) neurons relative to induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived (‘young’) neurons from the same donor fibroblasts, with significant enrichment of RNA binding proteins among the affected genes.These findings position APA as not only a novel layer of post-transcriptional regulation in ALS, but as a key mechanism by which neurons regulate gene expression in response to injury and aging.
